audit_scope.description: Trust model analysis for Ethereum Execution Layer components including P2P networking, precompiled contracts, and EVM opcodes. This batch covers historical hard fork transitions, cryptographic precompiles (BLS12-381, SHA256, KZG point evaluation), and EOF-related opcodes.

trusted_external_entities.name: P2P Network Peer
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Network peers are untrusted entities that can be operated by anyone on the public network. They propagate blocks and transactions which must be validated against consensus rules. Malicious peers could send invalid blocks, incorrect state data, or attempt DoS attacks. All data from peers must be cryptographically verified and validated before acceptance.

boundary_edges.security_assumption: All blocks received from peers are validated against fork-specific consensus rules (e.g., Homestead rules after block 1,150,000). Invalid blocks are rejected. The EL assumes that sufficient honest majority exists in the network to prevent long-range reorganizations.
boundary_edges.data_flow: Network peer sends block data via P2P protocol → EL validates block header, transactions, and state transition → Block is either accepted into chain or rejected
boundary_edges.attack_surface: Malformed blocks, invalid transactions, consensus rule violations, eclipse attacks, DoS via resource exhaustion

notes: 8 entities from the source files were identified as misclassified - they represent internal EL components (smart contracts, EOAs) rather than true external entities crossing the system boundary
Only 1 genuine external entity was found: network peers in the P2P layer

The precompiled contracts (BLS12-381, SHA256, KZG point evaluation) and EVM opcodes (EXTCODEADDRESS) all operate within the EL boundary and receive inputs from internal smart contracts, not external entities
The trust boundary for precompiles is at the contract invocation level, where untrusted contract code provides inputs, but this is internal to the EL execution environment
All identified external entities have corresponding boundary edges with security assumptions documented
